quote: Theorem 4: Let Y ~ EIPLD(alpha_1, beta_1, theta_1) and Z ~ EIPLD(alpha_2, beta_2, theta_2). If beta_1 = beta_2 and theta_2 >= theta_1 (or if beta_2 >= beta_1 and theta_1 = theta_2) then (Y <=lr Z) for all z. ... Setting alpha_1 = alpha_2. Case 1: for beta_1 = beta_2 and theta_2 >= theta_1 we obtained d/dz [g_Z(z)/g_Y(z)] as an increasing function of z. Case 2: beta_2 >= beta_1 and theta_1 = theta_2 we obtained d/dz [g_Z(z)/g_Y(z)] as an increasing function of z. This implies that Y <=lr Z for all z. Hence Y <=hr Z, Y <=mrl Z and Y <=st Z.

quote: A random variable Z is said to be greater than Y in the: (a) Stochastic order (Y <=st Z) if G_Z(z) <= G_Y(z) for all z; (b) Hazard rate order (Y <=hr Z) if h_Z(z) <= h_Y(z) for all z; (c) Mean residual order (Y <=mlr Z) if m_Z(z) <= m_Y(z) for all z; (d) Likelihood ratio order (Y <=lr Z) if g_Z(z)/g_Y(z) is an increasing function of z. The following results (Shaked and Shanthikumar 1994) are well known: Z <=lr Y => Z <=hr Y => Z <=mrl Y => Z <=st Y.
family: Exponentiated Inverse Power Lindley distribution EIPLD(alpha, beta, theta)
